facts.statehood_note: President Eisenhower's proclamation admitted Alaska as the 49th state.
facts.motto: North to the Future (chosen in 1967 for the Alaska Purchase Centennial)
borders: Gulf of Alaska and Pacific Ocean

symbols.name: Willow ptarmigan (light brown in summer, snow white in winter)

facts.name_origin: From the Aleut (Unangax) word "Alyeska," meaning "great land" (the state also explains it as an Aleut word for "the mainland").

government.legislature: Alaska State Legislature (meets at the State Capitol in Juneau)
government.chambers: Alaska Senate (20 senators, four-year terms) and Alaska House of Representatives (40 representatives, two-year terms) (Alaska Constitution, Article II)
government.executive: Governor (four-year term; after two full terms in a row, a governor must sit out a full term before running again). The governor heads the state's executive branch.
government.courts: Alaska Supreme Court (5 justices, who choose a chief justice for a three-year term); Court of Appeals (4 judges); Superior Court (45 judges, the main trial court); District Court (20 judges) with magistrate judges.
government.local: Alaska uses boroughs instead of counties. There are 19 organized boroughs (11 are home-rule boroughs, and 4 of those are unified municipalities that combine city and borough). Everywhere else is the Unorganized Borough, which has no borough government of its own; it covers more than half of Alaska's land but only about 10.5 percent of its people. Alaska also has 145 city governments.
government.constitution: Written by 55 delegates (49 men and 6 women) at the University of Alaska near Fairbanks, November 8, 1955, to February 6, 1956; ratified by voters on April 24, 1956 (17,447 to 8,180); took effect at statehood on January 3, 1959. Frank Peratrovich (Tlingit) was the only Alaska Native delegate.
government.kid_line: "All political power is inherent in the people. All government originates with the people, is founded upon their will only, and is instituted solely for the good of the people as a whole." (Alaska Constitution, Article I, Section 2)

long_ago.about: The Tlingit live in the temperate rainforest of Southeast Alaska. Salmon is one of their most important foods, and long ago salmon streams were owned by clans. Tlingit society has two halves, Raven and Eagle (also called Wolf); children belong to their mother's clan, up to 50 clan members lived in one house, and southern Tlingit raised tall totem poles in front of their houses.

The Unangax (Unangan, meaning "people") live in the Aleutian Islands. Historians estimate 8,000 to 10,000 or more people lived there when Russians arrived in the 1700s. They hunted seals, sea lions, and whales from small skin boats and lived in partly underground barabara houses.

The Yup'ik live in the Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta and along Bristol Bay. Families spent spring and summer at fish camps for salmon, and in winter the qasgiq (men's house) was the center for ceremonies, dancing, and storytelling.

Alaska's Athabascan peoples are descendants of the first people of the Interior. Eleven groups are known by their languages, and they lived by river and creek fishing and hunting; the Dena'ina also fished the coast of Cook Inlet.

today.about: Tsimshian families paddled canoes from British Columbia to Annette Island in 1887; Congress made the island a federal Indian reservation in 1891, and the Annette Island Reserve is Alaska's only federal Indian reservation (federally recognized).

today.nation: Central Council of the Tlingit and Haida Indian Tribes of Alaska
today.about: Founded in 1935, it is one of the two federally recognized regional tribes in Alaska, serving Tlingit and Haida citizens.

first_peoples.today_note: Alaska has 229 federally recognized tribes, most of them village tribes; the Bureau of Indian Affairs keeps the official list. Alaska Native people were 15.2 percent of Alaskans in the 2020 census. The Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act, signed December 18, 1971, kept about 44 million acres for Alaska Natives and paid about $963 million, through 12 regional corporations in Alaska (plus a 13th) and over 200 village corporations; it ended the earlier reservations except Metlakatla, which chose to stay out.
sites: Sitka National Historical Park (site of the 1804 Battle of Sitka; the K'alyaan Pole honors Tlingit who died)
The Aleutian and Pribilof Islands, Unangax homelands where majority-Aleut communities still live
Upward Sun River site in the Tanana Valley, where archaeologists found remains of an 'Ancient Beringian' infant in 2013

history.event: Indigenous peoples have lived in Alaska for thousands of years. Many scientists believe the region was the entry point for the first people of the Americas, by way of the Bering land bridge.

Russian expeditions led by Vitus Bering and Alexei Chirikov reach Alaska; Bering's crew lands on Kayak Island. The records of this voyage are generally accepted as the first European arrival in Alaska.

Russian fur hunters (promyshlenniki) force Unangax (Aleut) men to hunt sea otters and seals for them, often taking them away against their will. Disease and hardship hit hard: by 1830 the Unangax population had fallen by about 69 to 76 percent.

Grigory Shelikhov's men attack Alutiiq (Sugpiaq) men, women, and children at Refuge Rock on Sitkalidak Island, then found Russia's first permanent settlement in Alaska, a trading post at Three Saints Bay on Kodiak Island.
Russian navigator Gavriil Pribylov moves Unangax people to the Pribilof Islands as forced labor for the fur seal harvest.
The Russian emperor gives the Russian-American Company, formed by Shelikhov's heirs and other traders, sole rights to the fur trade in Alaska.
Tlingit warriors attack and destroy the Russian post at Old Sitka.

In the Battle of Sitka (October 1–4), Russians attack the Kiks.ádi Tlingit fort led by war chief K'alyaan. The Kiks.ádi retreat north at night, and the Russians build New Archangel (Sitka), the capital of Russian America.

On March 30, the U.S. agrees to buy Alaska from Russia for $7.2 million (about 2 cents an acre). About 50,000 Alaska Natives then lived outside Russian control. On October 18 (now Alaska Day), the U.S. flag is raised at Sitka.
The U.S. Army governs the new Department of Alaska; the Treasury Department takes over in 1877.
Alaska becomes the 49th state on January 3 (outside the 1877 arc, included for statehood).

trailblazers.name: K'alyaan (Katlian)
trailblazers.text: K'alyaan led the Kiks.ádi Tlingit defense of their fort at Shís'gi Noow in the 1804 Battle of Sitka against Russian forces. When the fort could not hold, the clan escaped at night on a long march north. The K'alyaan Pole at Sitka National Historical Park honors the Tlingit who died.

trailblazers.name: Elizabeth Peratrovich
trailblazers.text: Peratrovich helped win the Alaska Equal Rights Act of 1945, the first state anti-discrimination law in the United States. It guaranteed all Alaskans equal use of public places and businesses and banned segregation signs.

trailblazers.name: Frank Peratrovich
trailblazers.text: Frank Peratrovich was the only Alaska Native among the 55 delegates who wrote Alaska's constitution at the University of Alaska in 1955 and 1956.

trailblazers.name: William A. Egan
trailblazers.text: Egan led the convention that wrote Alaska's constitution and became the state's first governor after statehood in 1959.

trailblazers.name: Emil Notti
trailblazers.text: In 1966 Notti called the statewide meeting that grew into the Alaska Federation of Natives, and he became its full-time president in 1967. The federation's ideas shaped the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act of 1971.

landforms: Aleutian Islands (more than 1,200 miles into the Pacific)
Volcanoes such as Mount Shishaldin and Mount Spurr
Bering Glacier (largest glacier in North America, 2,008 square miles)
waters: Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta (one of the largest river deltas in the world)
Turnagain Arm (tides of more than 35 feet)
geography.regions: Alaska's regions are Southeast (the rainy Inside Passage), Southcentral (Anchorage and the Kenai Peninsula), the Interior (the largest region, with Fairbanks and Denali), Southwest (Kodiak Island and the Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta), the Aleutians, and the Arctic North Slope.

ecosystems.name: Southeast temperate rainforest
ecosystems.about: Ketchikan averages over 150 inches of rain and snow a year. The region holds the Tongass National Forest, the largest national forest in the United States, with Sitka spruce, the state tree.

ecosystems.name: Arctic tundra
ecosystems.about: Tundra covers the North Slope, north of the Brooks Range. Alaska is home to 112 kinds of mammals, including polar bears, caribou, and gray wolves.

ecosystems.name: Rivers, deltas, and salmon
ecosystems.about: Five kinds of salmon (sockeye, chinook, coho, pink, and chum) swim Alaska's rivers, feeding people, bears, and birds; more than 500 bird species have been recorded in Alaska.

science.weather: Alaska is the coldest state. Interior winters can drop below -60°F; the record low is -80°F at Prospect Creek (1971) and the record high is 100°F at Fort Yukon (1915). Hazards include earthquakes, tsunamis, landslides, volcanic eruptions along the Aleutians, and extreme cold.
science.resources: Oil and gas provide more than 80 percent of state government revenue (Prudhoe Bay on the North Slope), and seafood such as salmon, cod, pollock, and crab is Alaska's main export besides oil and gas.
science.highlight: The 1964 Good Friday earthquake (magnitude 9.2) shook for 4 minutes and 38 seconds, the fourth most powerful earthquake in recorded history. A 27-foot tsunami destroyed the village of Chenega, and some land near Kodiak rose 30 feet.

g3_ss.title: Alaska's Communities and Government
g3_ss.plan: Map Juneau, Anchorage, Fairbanks, and Sitka; learn the Legislature (20 senators, 40 representatives), the governor, and the 5-justice Supreme Court; compare boroughs to counties; read Article I, Section 2.

g3_ss.title: Alaska's First Peoples
g3_ss.plan: Compare how the Tlingit, Unangax, Yup'ik, and Athabascan peoples used rainforest, sea, delta, and river; learn one word or tradition from each.

g3_ss.title: Alaska Trailblazers
g3_ss.plan: Elizabeth Peratrovich and the 1945 Equal Rights Act, K'alyaan at Sitka, and Frank Peratrovich at the constitutional convention; make a 'stand up for fairness' card.

g45_ss.title: Alaska's First Nations
g45_ss.plan: The Bering land bridge idea, Ancient Beringians at Upward Sun River, and the homelands and ways of life of Alaska Native peoples.

g45_ss.title: Russian America
g45_ss.plan: Bering and Chirikov (1741), forced labor and disease among the Unangax, Three Saints Bay (1784), the Russian-American Company (1799), and Tlingit resistance at Sitka (1802 and 1804).

g45_ss.title: From Purchase to Statehood
g45_ss.plan: The 1867 purchase and Alaska Day, Army rule (1867–1877), then a leap forward to the 1945 Equal Rights Act, the 1955–56 constitution, and statehood in 1959.

g3_sci.title: Life on the Tundra
g3_sci.plan: Cold-climate adaptations: willow ptarmigan color change, caribou, polar bears, and permafrost ground.

g3_sci.title: Salmon Journeys
g3_sci.plan: Life cycle of the five Alaska salmon and the animals and people who depend on them.

g3_sci.title: Glaciers and Ice
g3_sci.plan: How glaciers form and move, using the Bering Glacier as the example.

g45_sci.title: Earthquakes, Volcanoes, and Tsunamis
g45_sci.plan: Plate edges along the Aleutians; the 1964 magnitude 9.2 earthquake and Chenega tsunami; how to stay safe.

g45_sci.title: Extreme Weather and Climate
g45_sci.plan: Compare -80°F Prospect Creek with rainy Ketchikan; why latitude and mountains change climate.

g45_sci.title: Rainforest to Tundra Ecosystems
g45_sci.plan: Food webs in the Tongass rainforest versus the North Slope tundra.
